procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Magistrate acquitting the respondent (Ghisa Ram)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Municipal Corporation) filed an appeal against the Magistrate's order of acquittal before the Punjab High Court, Circuit Bench at Delhi. The High Court upheld the order of the Magistrate.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (Municipal Corporation) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the report of the Public Analyst ceases to be evidence of the facts contained in it if a certificate from the Director of the Central Food Laboratory cannot be obtained for any reason.

facts: A food inspector took a sample of curd from the respondent, which was divided into three parts. One was given to the respondent, and one was sent to the Public Analyst.
The Public Analyst's report, which found the sample to be adulterated, was issued on October 23, 1961.
The prosecution filed a complaint against the respondent seven months later, on May 23, 1962.
The respondent exercised his right under s. 13(2) of the Act to have his sample sent to the Director of the Central Food Laboratory.
The Director reported that the sample had become highly decomposed and could not be analyzed, thus no certificate was issued.
law: Under s. 13(3) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, a certificate issued by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory supersedes the report of the Public Analyst.
Under s. 13(5), the Director's certificate is considered final and conclusive evidence of the facts stated within it.
Section 13(2) of the Act confers a valuable right on the accused to have their sample analyzed by the Director for the purpose of their defense.
application: The Supreme Court first established that, as a legal principle, the report of the Public Analyst does not cease to be evidence simply because a certificate from the Director of the Central Food Laboratory cannot be obtained. The Analyst's report is only superseded if the Director actually performs an analysis and issues a certificate.

However, the Court then examined the reason why the Director's certificate was not available. It found that the prosecution's "inordinate delay" of seven months in filing the complaint was the direct cause of the sample decomposing.
This delay deprived the respondent of his valuable statutory right under s. 13(2) to have his sample tested by a more competent expert, whose certificate would have been conclusive evidence.
The Court reasoned that when the accused is denied this right due to the deliberate conduct or laches of the prosecution, it causes serious prejudice to their defense.

Therefore, while the Public Analyst's report technically remained evidence in the case, the Court held that it would be improper to uphold a conviction based on it when the accused's ability to challenge that evidence was frustrated by the prosecution's own actions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the absolute proposition that the Public Analyst's report ceases to be evidence if the Director's certificate is unobtainable. However, it held that if the inability to obtain the Director's certificate is a result of the prosecution's own conduct (such as inordinate delay) which denies the accused a valuable right and prejudices their defense, a conviction cannot be sustained on the basis of the Public Analyst's report alone.

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused can be convicted on the basis of a Public Analyst's report when they have been denied their statutory right under s. 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, to have their sample analysed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory due to inordinate delay by the prosecution in launching the case.

facts: A food sample was taken from the respondent, divided into three parts, and one part was given to the respondent.
The Public Analyst's report was received, but the prosecution waited seven months before filing a complaint against the respondent.
After the prosecution was launched, the respondent exercised their right under s. 13(2) of the Act to have their sample analysed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The Director of the CFL reported that the sample had become "highly decomposed and could not be analysed" due to the long delay.
law: Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, confers a valuable statutory right on an accused to have their sample analysed by the Director of the CFL.
A certificate from the Director of the CFL supersedes the report of the Public Analyst and is considered final and conclusive evidence.
If, for any reason, the Director cannot issue a certificate, the Public Analyst's report does not automatically cease to be evidence.
However, a distinction is made for cases where the accused's right is denied due to the deliberate conduct or inaction of the prosecution.
application: The Court found that the prosecution's "inordinate delay" of seven months in filing the complaint was the direct cause of the sample's decomposition.
This delay effectively denied the respondent their valuable right to challenge the Public Analyst's report with a certificate from a more authoritative expert (the Director of the CFL).

The Court reasoned that the prosecution should have anticipated potential delays and taken the elementary precaution of adding a preservative to the sample, which would have prevented its decomposition.
By failing to act promptly and take necessary precautions, the prosecution's conduct seriously prejudiced the respondent's ability to mount a proper defense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that an accused cannot be convicted on the basis of a Public Analyst's report when they have been denied their valuable statutory right under s. 13(2) due to the deliberate conduct and inordinate delay of the prosecution. This denial caused serious prejudice to the accused's defense, and therefore, the acquittal was justified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the report of the Public Analyst ceases to be evidence of the facts contained in it if a certificate from the Director of the Central Food Laboratory cannot be obtained for any reason.
appellant_arguments: The absence of a certificate from the Director of the Central Food Laboratory for any reason does not affect the value, efficacy, or evidentiary status of the report given by the Public Analyst.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's defense implied that the inability to obtain the superseding certificate from the Director rendered the Public Analyst's report insufficient for a valid conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused can be convicted on the basis of a Public Analyst's report when they have been denied their statutory right under s. 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, to have their sample analysed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory due to inordinate delay by the prosecution in launching the case.
appellant_arguments: The conviction should be upheld based on the Public Analyst's report, which remains valid evidence regardless of the inability to get a certificate from the Director.
respondent_arguments: The respondent could not be validly convicted because the inordinate delay by the prosecution in launching the case denied them their valuable statutory right to have the sample analyzed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory.
This denial of a right, which only accrues after prosecution is initiated, was due to the sample decomposing over the long period of delay, and this seriously prejudiced the respondent's defense.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where the prosecution's conduct, such as an inordinate delay in launching proceedings, denies an accused the valuable statutory right to have their sample analyzed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory, the accused is so seriously prejudiced in their defense that a conviction based on the Public Analyst's report cannot be sustained.
obiter: The report of the Public Analyst does not cease to be evidence or become ineffective merely because a certificate from the Director of the Central Food Laboratory cannot be obtained for any reason.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the report of a Public Analyst does not cease to be evidence merely because a superseding certificate from the Director of the Central Food Laboratory cannot be obtained, a conviction cannot be sustained on the basis of that report if the accused has been denied their valuable statutory right under s. 13(2) of the Act to obtain such a certificate due to the deliberate conduct and inordinate delay of the prosecution. In such circumstances, the accused is so seriously prejudiced in their trial that it would not be proper to uphold the conviction, as the denial of this right is a result of the prosecution's own actions.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the accused was denied the valuable right under s. 13(2) to have their sample analyzed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory.
Whether the denial of this right was a result of the deliberate conduct or inordinate laches of the prosecution.
Whether the denial of this right seriously prejudiced the accused in their defense.
why_appellant_lost: The prosecution committed inordinate and unexplained delay by filing the complaint approximately seven months after receiving the Public Analyst's report.

This delay directly caused the denial of the respondent's statutory right, as the sample decomposed during this period, making it impossible for the Director of the Central Food Laboratory to analyze it.

The prosecution failed to take the elementary precaution of adding a preservative to the sample, which could have prevented its decomposition and preserved the respondent's right to have it re-analyzed.

The court found that the conviction could not be sustained because the respondent was prejudiced in his defense and denied a valuable right of defending himself solely due to the deliberate acts of the prosecution.
why_respondent_won: The respondent was deprived of the valuable statutory right conferred by s. 13(2) of the Act to have the sample given to him analyzed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory, whose certificate would have superseded the Public Analyst's report.
This right is a valuable one for the accused's proper defense, as the Director is a greater expert whose certificate is treated as conclusive evidence.
The denial of this right was not the respondent's fault but was caused entirely by the inordinate delay of the prosecution in launching the case, which allowed the sample to decompose.
The court held that the denial of this right due to the prosecution's conduct seriously prejudiced the respondent's trial, thus vitiating the conviction.
policy_considerations: When a valuable right is conferred by statute on an accused for their proper defense, it is expected that the prosecution will proceed in such a manner that the right will not be denied to them.

The right to have a sample analyzed by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory is a valuable safeguard for the accused, allowing them to challenge the Public Analyst's findings with a conclusive report from a more competent expert.

A conviction is vitiated when the prosecution's own conduct, such as inordinate delay, results in the denial of a statutory right to the accused, as this constitutes a serious prejudice to the principles of a fair trial.
